title: Princess Sun Tama / Ann Harding Murdock
summary: Princess Sun Tama, also known as Ann Harding Murdock, was an elected Matinecock spokesperson whose work connected community organization, land-rights advocacy, political representation, and continuing Matinecock presence.
content:
Princess Sun Tama, also known as Ann Harding Murdock and Ann H. Murdock, was an elected spokesperson for the Matinecock community. Her public work joined community organization, political representation, land-rights advocacy, and the continued assertion of Matinecock presence on Long Island.1

Community organization in Douglaston

On May 31, 1958, Ann Harding Murdock and her sister Lila Elizabeth Harding, known as Princess Brown Thrush, helped organize a Matinecock gathering at Zion Episcopal Church in Douglaston. Donna Gentle Spirit Barron records that more than 300 descendants and supporters filled the church and that John H. “Standing Waters” Waters was installed as senior chieftain. The gathering elected Princess Sun Tama as spokesperson. In Barron’s account, she explained that the community had been quiet for many years and that the time had come to unite again.2

Princess Sun Tama later conducted tribal affairs from a Flushing headquarters. Public reporting connected that work with a specific address, but this article keeps the location broad because surviving records also associate the address with a residence.

A letter asserting Matinecock land rights

On January 25, 1969, Princess Sun Tama and the Matinecock council sent Huntington officials a letter protesting the town’s use of land and underwater territory that the community said it had never sold or given away. The Long Island Press reported the letter on February 7. The letter placed Matinecock political identity and land claims in the present rather than treating them as a closed colonial subject.3

Confronting Huntington officials

In March 1969, Princess Sun Tama led a delegation to Huntington Town Hall. According to The Long-Islander, the delegation asserted Matinecock ownership from Cold Spring Harbor to Northport Harbor and south toward Melville. She challenged the town’s reliance on a 1653 transaction, arguing that the promised payment of wampum had not been made, and called for recognition, an accounting, and land for community use. These were the Matinecock delegation’s claims as reported at the time; the newspaper and town responses should not be mistaken for neutral descriptions of Matinecock title or governance.4

Continuing leadership

Princess Sun Tama died later in 1969. John A. Strong records that Princess Brown Thrush succeeded her as spokesperson. Decades later, Chief Osceola Townsend described his advocacy as a continuation of the struggle Princess Sun Tama had begun. That continuity matters: her work was not a brief revival of a vanished community, but part of an ongoing Matinecock political history.5

References

  • Donna Gentle Spirit Barron, The Long Island Indians and Their New England Ancestors (2006), pp. 88–89.
  • “Indians Claim Huntington,” Long Island Press, February 7, 1969, p. 1.
  • “Indians Assert Claim to Land,” The Long-Islander, March 20, 1969.
  • “Indians Complain of Town Brush Off,” The Long-Islander, 1969.
  • John A. Strong, “The Reaffirmation of Tradition Among the Native Americans of Eastern Long Island,” Long Island Historical Journal 7, no. 1 (Fall 1994), p. 25.
  • John A. Strong, We Are Still Here! The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island Today (1998), p. 68.
why_this_matters: Princess Sun Tama’s leadership shows Matinecock political life continuing through community organization, public testimony, land-rights advocacy, and demands for municipal recognition in the twentieth century.
activity_update_summary: Added a broader source-supported biography of Princess Sun Tama, including the 1958 Douglaston gathering, her election as Matinecock spokesperson, the 1969 Huntington letter and delegation, succession, and mapped Historic Moments.
